Microcirculation is exactly where the capillaries are doing a U-turn, between arteries 
and veins. I call this the place of action because this is where microcirculation occurs. 
In another words, you don’t have microcirculation at the four large arteries. And 
every cell needs capillaries for supply. We are dealing with a totally new group of 
blood vessels that has no tunica media and no tunica externa. So therefore, 
classification, what we used to do with tunica media doesn’t work anymore. 
Classification is going to be based on how leaky the capillaries are. Some capillaries 
are going to have pericytes, some don’t, because that also contributes to the 
leakiness. In different books this is what you find, there are 50,000 miles of 
capillaries; that means about 10-20 billion capillaries to supply every single cell for 
oxygen and nutrients.

First we’re going to cover endothelial cells. I don’t want to read my slides, I just want 
to point out to you the most important things. First of all, look at the image below. 
You have to imagine if I was in the classroom I would hold a piece of white paper in 
my hands and roll it up, that’s basically it. The roll up could be one endothelial cell, or 
it could be several endothelial cells next to each other. You guys remember, these are 
squamous epithelial cells, and you can see them from a longitudinal view, but in our 
slides you’ll see them mostly as a cross-sectional view; and the nucleus is going to be 
kind of flat, little bit pushed into the lumen but the only reason for that is the nucleus 
is a bit thicker than the surrounding cytoplasm. But I want to make another point, 
since we don’t have tunica media we don’t have vascular smooth muscle, so there is 
no vasoconstriction here at all. So this nucleus is not going to budge into the lumen 
and become round like what we saw in the arterioles. We already talked about the 
function the other day, this is the end result of the branchy branchy system in order 
to create the thinnest wall in the body so that we can do microcirculation, or 
exchange, in other words, oxygen/CO2 exchange and nutrient/waste exchange. What 
else can endothelial cells do? They are selective blood-tissue barriers. Selective 
means that they can selectively transport some molecules, barrier means that, and I 
told you this many times, number one function of any kind of epithelium including 
endothelium is that there’s no leakage. And since we’re dealing with blood, no

we are looking inside the endothelial cell (right picture) obviously you cannot see the

the tissue cells, and back and forth. When we give you the supply this is the route. 
When we are picking up the waste and CO2, the route is the opposite: tissue cells, 
interstitial fluid, back to blood through the endothelial wall.

This slide is going to show you what we talked about earlier, the weibel-palade bodies 
of the endothelial cells. Now the weibel-palade is named after the three guys here as 
you can see. No need to memorize, I just wanted you to have an input of history here. 
What is this fellow? You see here (in the picture) it’s labeled WP? One, two, three of 
them. It’s electron-dense, which means dark, rod-like, specialized membrane bound 
organelles inside the endothelial cells. They are storing two kinds of protein. And 
where is this guy located? In the cytoplasm of the endothelium. So what is the von 
WILLEBRAND factor, which is made out of glycoproteins? If the endothelium gets 
damaged, for whatever reason, this factor gets released by the endothelial cells and 
will increase platelet adhesion at the site of the endothelial injury. In another words, 
trying to patch the hole on the wall. Protein 2 is P-selectin protein. If there is an 
inflammation infection or tissue damage, P-selectin is released by the endothelial 
cells and starts initiating migration/exit of neutrophils from the blood to the infected 
connective tissue. We’re going to see this on another slide.

So far we covered what the endothelial cells are doing all day long and how they look, 
structure, function, location. Now we’re going to focus on capillaries, what is the 
definition and general features. Definition based on being the end product of 
branchy-branchy. This is where the arteries end, there is a U-turn, and this is where 
the veins begin. So technically, the capillary beds have a red or arterial side, which is 
the branchy-branchy from the arteriole; and they have a blue venous side, which is 
the mergy-mergy toward the post-capillary venule. We already did all this actually, 
thinnest wall has the highest permeability. However, anytime you have a thin wall it’s 
good for permeability, but it’s not good for protection. Whenever you have a thick 
wall, like your skin, it’s very good for protection but it’s not very good for 
permeability. The capillaries have a diameter of 5-10 microns, this is a very good 
number to remember because this is kind of like a ruler for you to remember to 
compare them with other kinds of cells or structures in the body. For example, the 
erythrocyte is about 7 microns, you see? So the narrowest capillaries are smaller than 
erythrocytes, so the erythrocytes often pass in a single line. I believe you can kind of 
see it here. They are going like what I call a kindergarten field trip. Sometimes if they 
are bigger, 7 microns in a 5 micron capillary, they need to fold, the red blood cell is 
flexible and it can fold on itself to get through the capillary. So why are the 
erythrocytes pressed against the capillary wall very tightly? So we can reduce the 
7
Capillary: Definition and General Features
Definition based on being the end product of branchy-branchy: 
• Where arteries end: branching into the “red" or arterial side of capillaries
• U-turn
• Where veins begin: merging/draining from the “blue” or venous side of the capillaries
Smallest microscopic vessels
Thinnest wall (most vulnerable to high blood pressure)
• highest permeability-weakest protection
Smallest diameter blood vessels
• Capillary diameter is 5–10 microns, close to the diameter of an erythrocyte (7 microns). The narrowest capillaries are smaller than an 
erythrocyte, so erythrocytes pass in single file (kindergarten fieldtrip) and sometimes fold to get through
• Why is the erythrocyte pressed against the capillary wall? Reduce the distance for oxygen to diffuse from the erythrocyte to the tissue cell
Longest: 50 000 miles
Largest number: 10-20 billion capillaries (for 30 trillion cells)
The human body contains approximately 30 trillion cells. About 90% are red blood cells circulating in the blood. 
The remaining 3 trillion cells make up the body’s tissues and depend on blood capillaries for the exchange of oxygen, nutrients, and wastes

This is microcirculation, what you see in front of you. The routes of exchange 
between blood and the tissue cells. This is the arteriole, which is the last artery, the 
smallest artery, microscopic artery. And it creates branchy to make capillaries. You see 
this is the red side of the capillary, or arteriole side. This is where the supply is coming 
out of, from the blood to the cells. From the capillary lumen, crossing the endothelial 
wall and basal lamina (if it’s there), then interstitial fluid in the connective tissues, 
and then into the tissue cells, whatever cells we need to keep alive. Even in the 
connective tissue we need to keep the fibroblasts alive. So what is moving here? The 
oxygen, the nutrients in the interstitial fluid. Let’s see on the venous side. You see the 
arrows are coming back? We are removing the waste from the cells and delivering it 
back to the blood. So you have some tissue cells in the neighborhood, and the CO2 
and the waste is going to enter the blue side of the capillary, crossing the endothelial 
wall, then mergy-mergy into the venule, and we already know the first venule is the 
post-capillary venule. Number three, do you remember that the lymphatic system is 
here to pick up what the blue side of the capillary left behind. It doesn’t pick up 
everything. Dr Moni will explain to you the pressures related to that. But basically 
some of the excess interstitial fluid, proteins, and waste products will enter the 
lymphatic capillary system. If it doesn’t happen, then edema can develop and fluid-
buildup can happen here in the interstitial space.

Let me just summarize it again. So we started out with endothelial cells, then we 
continued to capillaries, and now we are moving to capillary beds. That’s what you 
see in front of you. First of all, a true capillary bed is an interwoven network of 
capillaries for supplying. But what is really interesting is one arteriole is capable of 
branchy-branchy into 10-100 capillaries. Here you see, like, 5, but it could be 10-100 
capillaries. And of course on the blue side it’s the mergy-mergy. Don’t forget that the 
lymphatic capillaries are also sitting here. See the blood capillaries’ U-turn, the blood 
goes down and makes a U-turn (what is she saying here SOS) and then go back on

vacuum cleaners sucking up the interstitial fluid and whatever is dissolved in it, back 
into the lymphatic capillaries, and eventually the lymphatic system delivers it back to 
the veins because the veins are the ones left behind.

I also wanted to touch on this traditional blood flow by capillaries. This is done by the 
autonomic nervous system, the distribution of blood in capillaries. Distribution means 
where most of the blood is. Let’s say the capillaries are all open. If I ask you, during 
exercise do you think the skeletal muscle needs more oxygen and the capillaries are 
open? I think you would say yes. What about during digestion? Will the capillary bed 
be open if the small intestine just received a huge hamburger and you are digesting? 
The answer is yes. So these are the two situations where most of the blood is going 
to move to the skeletal muscles or small intestine. These two things can actually clash 
with each other, that’s why you don’t want to get on the treadmill when you digest, 
because you want to keep the blood doing the food absorption in the small intestine. 
On the other side, the capillaries are closed. During digestion we want the blood in 
the intestine. During exercise we want the blood in the skeletal muscles.

Now we come to the classification of capillaries. Remember we cannot do the 
classification of capillaries by tunica media because we do not have tunica media. 
Therefore we’re going to classify them by how leaky they are. As a result, what type 
of molecules can go across the endothelial cells. We have to look at two things, the 
endothelial cell itself and the basement membrane, and then –this is continuous (first 
capillary) so this is going to be the least leaky, and you see (fenestrated) there are 
going to be holes on the endothelial cells but the basement membrane is going to be 
continuous so this is going to be more leaky, and then look at this (sinusoid) 
everybody is full of holes. There are intercellular gaps, or large fenestra, in the 
endothelial cells and the basement membrane is also incomplete. 
16
Classification of capillaries based on “leakiness”

Let’s look at the continuous capillaries. This is the one that’s least leaky. Basically the 
first sentence is the most important. Continuous endothelium, continuous basement 
membrane, and maybe this type of capillary has pericytes, a new type of cell. These 
somatic are also called somatic capillaries because they are in your body. They’re 
located in most body tissues, skin, lungs connective tissue, and you’ll read the rest of 
them later. Now let’s look at the image. Do you see how many endothelial cells I can 
see? There is a border here and there’s a border here, so this is one endothelial cell. 
Then there’s a border here, there’s a border here, so there’s the second endothelial 
cell. And border here, going going going, border here, so this is the third endothelial 
cell. And the knife didn’t go through the nucleus. In the neighborhood you can see 
fibroblasts, and you can see pericytes. And observe that the major function of 
pericytes is –pericytes have these arms that are technically hugging the capillary, 
supporting it. There’s a basement membrane labeled here, and usually the pericyte is 
within the shared basement membrane with the endothelium. However, some 
places, the pericyte may have its own basement membrane. Do you see how this is 
folding over here? This is called marginal folds. And you guys read the rest. So this is 
the least leaky, therefore only small molecules can go across, and lipid soluble 
molecules. Lipid soluble molecules can go through anything. For larger molecules you 
need pinocytic vesicles but I already showed you.


Posterior intercostal 
arteries & subcostal arteries

Superior phrenic arteries 

Pericardial, Esophageal 
and Bronchial arteries
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

[Automated OCR; verify medical terms against the original page.]
The descending aorta is called thoracic descending while it's running through the thorax. it supplies posterior
intercostal arteries, intercostal spaces from number 3 and all the way down. It also gives us superior phrenic
arteries to supply the diaphragm and small branches like pericardial, esophageal and bronchi to supply
respectively these internal organs. After it pierces the diaphragm at the level of T12 in abdominal cavity we
call it abdominal descending.

Pulmonary trunk

conveys deoxygenated 
blood from the right 
ventricle to the lungs

terminates in the concavity 
of the aortic arch
Branches:

Right pulmonary artery

Left pulmonary artery
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

[Automated OCR; verify medical terms against the original page.]
the pulmonary trunk is an artery which carries deoxygenated blood from the right
ventricle to the lungs. I would like to confirm that the important structure in
between the aorta and the pulmonary trunk is called ligamentum arteriosum.

Ligamentum arteriosum

It is a fibrous band that 
connects the bifurcation of 
the pulmonary trunk to the 
concavity of the aortic arch

It represents the remains of 
the ductus arteriosus 

Ductus arteriosus in the 
fetus conducts blood from 
the pulmonary trunk to the 
aorta, bypassing the lungs
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

[Automated OCR; verify medical terms against the original page.]
In embryological life this ligamentum arteriosum serves as a duct. This ductus arteriosus shunts the blood from
the pulmonary trunk to aorta. Before birth, the pressure is higher in the right side of the heart than in the left,
following the pressure gradient blood is shunted from pulmonary trunk to aorta. After birth, the pressure becomes
higher in the left side than the right so blood is shunted from aorta to pulmonary trunk. The high level of oxygen in
the blood from aorta to pulmonary trunk triggers the muscle walls of the ductus arteriosus to constrict. Over a
few days this constriction causes it to close completely and turn into a fibrous remnent called the ligamentum
arteriosum.

Patent ductus arteriosus 
(PDA)

It results from failure of the ductus 
arteriosus (a connection between the 
pulmonary trunk and aorta) to constrict 
and close after birth. 

Patients are present with a machine-like
diastolic and systolic murmur heard 
over the left sternoclavicular joint.

Prostaglandin E and low O2 tension 
sustain patency of the ductus arteriosus in 
the fetal period.

PDA is common in premature infants and in 
cases of maternal rubella infection. 

Left –to-right shunt increased pressure in 
pulmonary circulation (pulmonary 
hypertension) and is non-cyanotic

Treatment: surgical division and ligation
imperative. In great danger is left 
recurrent nerve (wrapping aorta arch). 
Injure of this nerve results in hoarseness. 
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

[Automated OCR; verify medical terms against the original page.]
what happens if this duct stays patent after birth? What kind of abnormality would you expect?
If the duct doesn't close before 74 to 78 hours the condition is called patent ductus arteriosus
What to expect from a patient who has this condition (symptoms):
Mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood because of the blood shunting from aorta to pulmonary trunk results
in non cyanotic defect.
Machine-like diastolic and systolic murmur which is heard best over the left sternoclavicular joint.
How to treat patient: it's a problem we find in premature newborns who lack oxygenation of blood so we provide
them with oxygen to help with the closure of the patent ductus arteriosus.
Prostaglandin E levels play an important role in the closure of this duct. By the end of the third trimester in pregnancy
the prostglandin e levels drop in mother's blood making the duct close.
Premature newborns with this condition have a high prostaglandin e level so we provide them with an antagonist to
help with the closure.
If oxygen and antagonist dont work we surgically close the patent ductus arteriosus.
You might accidentally ligate the left recurrent laryngeal nerve together with duct causing hoarseness of voice of
baby. (when surgery goes wrong )
Baby still cries but with hoarseness. It won't cause big shift in hemodynamics. No hypertension. <- answers to
students questions.
Question
An infant born 2 weeks premature presents with a machine-like diastolic and
systolic murmur heard over the left sternoclavicular joint. What will be observed
in the infant as a result of this defect?
A. There will be blood flow from the arch of the aorta into the pulmonary trunk
through the defect.
B. The pulmonary trunk will have a significantly smaller diameter than the
ascending aorta. tetrology of fallot
C. The infant will be cyanotic at birth. tetrology of fallot
D. There will be blood flow from the left ventricle to the right ventricle through the
defect. ventricular septal defect
E. The aorta overrides the interventricular septum and collects blood from both
the right and left ventricles. tetrology of fallot

ESOPHAGUS

Muscular tube extending from the 
superior mediastinum through 
the posterior mediastinum that 
serves to convey food from the 
pharynx to the stomach

It starts at the level of the cricoid 
cartilage (C6), pierces the 
diaphragm at the level of T10, 
and descends another inch before 
it becomes continuous with the 
stomach

Muscular wall consists of skeletal 
muscle in its upper third, 
smooth muscle in its lower
third, and a combination of both 
in the middle third
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

[Automated OCR; verify medical terms against the original page.]
Esophagus is placed in the superior mediastinum first running behind the trachea then behind the heart
in posterior mediastinum. It pierces the diaphragm at the level of T10. The terminal part of it is in the
abdominal cavity where it reaches the stomach. More info in GIT block.

Thoracic duct

Thoracic duct  (1) begins in 
the abdomen as a dilated sac, 
the cisterna chyli, and 
passes through the aortic 
opening

It enters the thorax in the 
posterior mediastinum to 
the right of the aorta 
ascends posterior & left to the 
esophagus joins the blood 
vascular system at the left 
venous angle (3) (junction 
of the left internal jugular and 
subclavian veins)
1
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

[Automated OCR; verify medical terms against the original page.]
Now, regarding the thoracic duct, we already reviewed today that it is a major lymphatic structure that
terminates at the left venous angle. We also know that it runs in the posterior mediastinum, the same
area where the esophagus and descending aorta are located

PHRENIC NERVES

Arises from the anterior branches of 
C3-C5 nerves and lies in front of 
the anterior scalene muscle.

Runs anterior to the root of the 
lung, whereas the vagus nerve
runs posterior to the root of the 
lung.

Is accompanied by the 
pericardiophrenic vessels of the 
internal thoracic vessels descending
between the mediastinal pleura and 
the pericardium.

Innervates the fibrous pericardium, 
the mediastinal and 
diaphragmatic pleurae (sensory 
innervation), and the diaphragm
for motor and its central tendon for 
sensory.
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

[Automated OCR; verify medical terms against the original page.]
The phrenic nerve arises from C3 to C5 segments of the spinal cord. It runs along the neck region first
anterior to the anterior scalene muscle. Then it becomes a structure in the superior mediastinum then it
becomes a structure in the middle mediastinum then it reaches the diaphragm.
For now i want you to know that the phrenic nerve is the only nerve which provides motor innervation
to the diaghragm. No other nerve makes the diaphragm contract.
It's a mixed nerve so it also has sensory fibres that innervate mediastinum, pleura, fibrous pericardium
of the heart and the sensory central tendon of the diaphragm. More info in next lecture

VAGUS NERVES

Descend from the neck in the 
thorax from the superior
through the posterior 
mediastinum where they 
form esophageal plexus

Together with the esophagus 
comes the abdominal cavity 
(T10) and forms two vagal 
trunks on the stomach

Anterior vagal trunk
terminates on the anterior 
wall of the stomach, 
posterior one along the left 
gastric artery comes to the 
celiac plexus to supply 
organs of the upper floor 
abdominal cavity
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

[Automated OCR; verify medical terms against the original page.]
The vagus nerve is the other major nerve in the thorax that runs in superior mediastinum and then
into the posterior mediastinum. It comes close to the esophagus in the lower part of the posterior
mediastinum forming esophageal plexus. The vagus nerve is a major parasympathetic structure that
provides parasympathetic innervation for all the organs in the thoracic cavity and many major organs
in the abdominal cavity. We will see the vagus nerve together with the esophagus go down to the
abdominal cavity where the right and left vagus nerves becomes anterior and posterior vagal trunks.

VAGUS NERVES
Branches in the thorax:

branches to the heart, lung, and 
esophagus

Left recurrent laryngeal nerve

approaches the aortic arch &
hooks around it lateral to the 
ligamentum arteriosum

ascends to the neck and supplies all 
the intrinsic muscles of the larynx, 
EXCEPT the cricothyroid (superior 
laryngeal nerve from cervical part 
vagus nerve supplies it)

Note: Right recurrent laryngeal
nerve arises from the right vagus at 
the root of the neck and hooks 
around the right subclavian 
artery
@ Dr. Olena, 2026

[Automated OCR; verify medical terms against the original page.]
In this slide i would like to confirm the important branches of the vagus
nerve, the recurrent laryngeal nerves. The left recurrent laryngeal nerve
forms a hook around the arch of aorta and the right recurrent laryngeal
nerve forms a hook around the subclavian artery. Both recurrent laryngeal
nerves go back to the larynx where they innervate all the muscles of the
larynx except cricothyroid muscle which is innervated by another branch of
the vagus nerve, the superior laryngeal nerve.

Transcribed by Haadiya Zeeshan
1
ANATOMY OF THE NOSE, 
LARYNX AND TRACHEA
DR. HASSAN SHAIBAH
Reviewed by Hassan Faiz

If you look at the surface anatomy of the nose, it will 
have a pyramid shape. The nose has a root which 
extends to your forehead, and it also has a dorsum. At 
the end of the dorsum, you have an apex. There are two 
openings at this apex called the nares. These nares lead 
to the vestibule, which is the area where the airflow 
comes. The two nares are separated into right and left 
by the nasal septum, which is made up of cartilages. 
2
SURFACE APPEARANCE 
THE EXTERNAL NOSE
 HAVE A PYRAMIDAL SHAPE. 
 NASAL ROOT LOCATED SUPERIORLY & 
CONTINUOUS WITH FOREHEAD. 
 APEX (1'6D,1)(5,25/<D,1D$D5281'('D¶7,3·’D
 SPANNING BETWEEN THE ROOT & APEX IS 
DORSUM OF THE NOSE.
 INFERIORLY TO APEX THE NARES; OPENINGS 
INTO THE VESTIBULE OF THE NASAL CAVITY. 
 NARES BOUNDED MEDIALLY BY NASAL 
SEPTUM, & LATERALLY BY ALA NASI (THE 
LATERAL CARTILAGINOUS WINGS OF THE 
NOSE).

If you look at this image, the nose is made up of a bony 
part and a cartilaginous part. The bony part (yellow) is 
the nasal bone. You have also the maxillary bone 
(brown). Your upper jaw contributes to the bony part of 
the nose. The rest of the area here is cartilage. You have 
lateral cartilages (green), one on the left side and one on 
the right side. You have septal cartilage (violet), the one 
which separates the right and left nares. You also have 
alar cartilage, because they look like a wing (a major and 
minor one). The rest here at the bottom is fatty tissue. 
3
SKELETAL STRUCTURE
MADE OF BONY & CARTILAGINOUS 
COMPONENTS:
 BONY COMPONENT ² LOCATED 
SUPERIORLY, COMPRISED OF 
CONTRIBUTIONS FROM NASAL, & 
MAXILLA BONES
 CARTILAGINOUS COMPONENT 
LOCATED INFERIORLY, COMPRISED: 
 2 LATERAL CARTILAGES 
 2 ALAR CARTILAGES 
 ONE SEPTAL CARTILAGE. 
 SOME SMALLER ALAR CARTILAGES

The nose is an organ that people can easily get bleeding 
from, because as you see in the image, it is very highly 
vascular. The nose receives arterial supply from different 
structures. There are branches of the face that are 
coming from different areas. We have the maxillary 
branches coming from maxillary. You also have branches 
from ophthalmic arteries. These contribute to all the 
blood supply to the nose. Also you have cartilages, which 
need vascularization to stay alive. One of the important 
arteries that gives nutrient supply to the septal cartilage 
is the angular artery, and also the lateral nasal artery. 
Both these arteries are coming from the facial artery. 
4
VESSELS AND LYMPHATICS
 EXTERNAL NOSE RECEIVES ARTERIAL SUPPLY FROM 

BRANCHES OF THE MAXILLARY (INFRA ORBITAL)  

OPHTHALMIC ARTERIES ( DORSAL & EXTERNAL )
 THE SEPTUM & ALAR CARTILAGES RECEIVE 
ADDITIONAL SUPPLY FROM ANGULAR ARTERY 
& LATERAL NASAL ARTERY. THESE ARE 
BOTH BRANCHES OF FACIAL ARTERY (DERIVED 
FROM EXTERNAL CAROTID ARTERY).
 VENOUS DRAINAGE IS INTO THE FACIAL VEIN, THEN 
IN TURN INTO INTERNAL JUGULAR VEIN.
 LYMPHATIC DRAINAGE FROM THE EXTERNAL NOSE IS 
VIA SUPERFICIAL LYMPHATIC VESSELS 
ACCOMPANYING THE FACIAL VEIN. THESE VESSELS, 
LIKE ALL LYMPHATIC VESSELS OF THE HEAD AND 
NECK, ULTIMATELY DRAIN INTO THE DEEP CERVICAL 
LYMPH NODES.

Venous drainage follows the arterial supply. Most of the 
veins drain into the facial vein -> internal jugular vein -> 
head -> heart. Lymphatic drainage comes from 
superficial lymph vessels and drains into deep cervical 
lymph nodes (in neck region). If somebody has infections 
in the face or nose, sometimes these lymph nodes get 
inflamed and you can get swelled.
4

Innervations is a favorite. Anything in the face is 
innervated by trigeminal nerve (sensations are coming 
from there). Trigeminal nerve is cranial nerve number 5 
and has three branches (V1, V2, and V3):

V1 (ophthalmic nerve) supplies anything above your 
upper eyelid and all the way on the above part of the 
skull. 

V2 (maxillary nerve) supplies your upper mandible, 
the nose area, and part of your cheek.

V3 (mandibular nerve) supplies the lower mandible.
5
INNERVATION
 SENSORY INNERVATION OF THE EXTERNAL NOSE IS DERIVED FROM THE TRIGEMINAL NERVE (CN V).
 EXTERNAL NASAL NERVE, A BRANCH OF OPHTHALMIC NERVE (CN V1), SUPPLIES THE SKIN OF THE 
DORSUM OF NOSE, NASAL ALAE AND NASAL VESTIBULE. 
 THE LATERAL ASPECTS OF THE NOSE ARE SUPPLIED BY THE INFRORBITAL NERVE, A BRANCH OF THE 
MAXILLARY NERVE (CN V2).

The nose comes between the V1 and V2 area, so it's 
sharing supply by part of V1 and part of V2 because it's 
between the eyes and part of the upper jaw. The 
external nerves are branches coming from these two 
branches of the trigeminal nerve. V1 gives the dorsum, 
vestibule, and part of the ala of the nose. V2 supplies the 
lateral aspect of the nose and the branch that is 
supplying it is the infraorbital nerve.
5

The nasal cavity has 3 regions: 
1) Olfactory region: Responsible for smell because it 
has olfactory cells and receptors. This is located at 
the top of the nose. 
2) Respiratory region: It is lined by pseudostratified 
epithelium and has many goblet cells that contribute 
to the secretion of the mucus that we need in this 
region. 
3) Vestibule: First region where air comes when you 
breathe in (then goes through the nares). It is the 
first area surrounding the external opening of the 
nose. 
6
THE NASAL CAVITY
 THE MOST SUPERIOR PART OF RESPIRATORY 
TRACT. 
 EXTENDS FROM VESTIBULE TO THE 
NASOPHARYNX, AND HAS THREE DIVISIONS:
1.
VESTIBULE ² THE AREA SURROUNDING 
ANTERIOR EXTERNAL OPENING TO NASAL 
CAVITY.
2.
RESPIRATORY REGION ² LINED BY 
CILIATED PSUDEOSTRATIFIED EPITHELIUM, 
WITH MUCUS-SECRETING GOBLET CELLS.
3.
OLFACTORY REGION ² LOCATED AT THE 
APEX OF THE NASAL CAVITY. LINED BY 
OLFACTORY CELLS & RECEPTORS.

Conchae (turbinates) are the bony part in the nose that 
contribute to the formation of shelf life. They are very 
important because they act like a turbine. When you 
breathe in, the air flows in a circular movement (not in a 
straight line). Below each conchae, there are openings 
we call the meatus. There are 3 meatuses:
1) Inferior meatus: Between inferior concha and the 
floor of the nose. 
2) Middle meatus: Between inferior and middle 
concha. 
3) Superior meatus: Between middle and the superior 
concha. 
7
NASAL CONCHAE
 LATERAL WALLS OF THE NASAL CAVITY CURVED 
SHELVES OF BONE. THEY ARE 
CALLED CONCHAE (OR TURBINATES). 
 3 CONCHAE ² INFERIOR, MIDDLE & SUPERIOR.
 PROJECT INTO NASAL CAVITY, CREATING 
PATHWAYS FOR THE AIR TO FLOW. THESE 
PATHWAYS ARE CALLED MEATUSES:
 INFERIOR MEATUS ² BETWEEN THE INFERIOR 
CONCHA AND FLOOR OF THE NASAL CAVITY.
 MIDDLE MEATUS ² BETWEEN THE INFERIOR AND 
MIDDLE CONCHA.
 SUPERIOR MEATUS ² BETWEEN THE MIDDLE AND 
SUPERIOR CONCHA.
 FUNCTION TO INCREASE THE SURFACE AREA OF 
THE NASAL CAVITY ² THIS INCREASES THE AMOUNT 
OF INSPIRED AIR, SO THAT IT CAN BE HUMIDIFIED.

There are some openings in this meatus, and this is very 
important. In my lecture, I like to refer to some 
important things that are usually a point of question in 
many USMLE exams. This is a very important point and 
is usually referred to in exam because these openings 
lead to a very important structure in your head. The 
middle meatus gives access to very important sinuses. 
The drainage of the frontal, maxillary, and ethmoidal 
sinuses are opening in this meatus. If a patient has 
blockage in one of these sinuses, the meatus gives you 
pathways to reach these sinuses. If these sinuses are 
blocked, you expect these pathways to be blocked and 
8
OPENINGS INTO THE NASAL CAVITY

ONE OF THE FUNCTIONS OF THE NOSE IS TO DRAIN A VARIETY OF 
STRUCTURES. MANY OPENINGS INTO NASAL CAVITY DRAINAGE 
OCCURS.

FRONTAL, MAXILLARY & ANTERIOR ETHMOIDAL SINUSES OPEN 
INTO MIDDLE MEATUS. THE LOCATION OF THIS OPENING IS 
MARKED BY THE SEMILUNAR HIATUS, A CRESCENT-SHAPED GROOVE 
ON THE LATERAL WALLS OF THE NASAL CAVITY.

MIDDLE ETHMOIDAL SINUSES EMPTY OUT ONTO A STRUCTURE 
CALLED THE ETHMOIDAL BULLA. 

THE POSTERIOR ETHMOIDAL SINUSES OPEN OUT AT THE LEVEL OF 
THE SUPERIOR MEATUS.

THE ONLY STRUCTURE NOT TO EMPTY OUT ONTO THE LATERAL 
WALLS OF THE NASAL CAVITY IS THE SPHENOID SINUS. IT DRAINS 
ONTO THE POSTERIOR ROOF.

IN ADDITION TO THE PARANASAL SINUSES, OTHER STRUCTURES 
OPEN INTO THE NASAL CAVITY:

NASOLACRIMAL DUCT ²DRAIN TEARS FROM THE EYE. IT OPENS INTO 
THE INFERIOR MEATUS.

AUDITORY (EUSTACHIAN) TUBE ² OPENS INTO THE NASOPHARYNX AT 
THE LEVEL OF THE INFERIOR MEATUS. IT ALLOWS THE MIDDLE EAR TO 
EQUALISE WITH THE ATMOSPHERIC AIR PRESSURE.

filled with mucus or hard stuff. That's why you need to 
open it in order for the patient to breathe properly. The 
ethmoidal bulla also open to the middle ethmoidal 
sinuses. The middle ethmoidal sinuses have an anterior, 
middle, and posterior part. Each part opens in a different 
area. The posterior part opens into the superior meatus. 
The sphenoid sinus opening into the posterior roof of 
the meatus. In addition to the paranasal sinus, there are 
other structures that open into these meatus. One of 
them is the nasolacrimal duct which drains into the 
inferior meatus. That's why if somebody has a problem 
with draining their tears into their nose, this is the 
pathway that the doctor needs to be opening for the 
patient in order for the tears to pass properly to the 
nose. One other structure that also opens near the 
inferior meatus is the Eustachian tubes. This allows the 
equalization of pressure between the air and middle ear.
8

The auditory tube connects the middle ear and the 
upper respiratory tract, which is why it could be a path 
of infections. That's why when people have problems or 
have common cold or have a lot of secretions, their 
hearing can be impacted. It is also why small children 
;ĞƐƉĞĐŝĂůůǇsŶĞǁďŽƌŶƐͿsƚŚĂƚsĚŽŶ͛ƚsŬŶŽǁsŚŽǁsƚŽsďůŽǁsƚŚĞŝƌs
nose have a lot of accumulated secretion in the nasal 
cavity. When they lay down, these secretions can travel 
to the middle ear and cause middle ear infection. So 
pediatricians tell parents if the kids have a common cold 
to slightly raise up the head of the baby in order for the 
mucus to drain down instead of going into the ear and 
9
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: SPREAD OF INFECTION
 AS THE AUDITORY TUBE CONNECTS THE MIDDLE EAR AND UPPER RESPIRATORY TRACT, IT IS A 
PATH BY WHICH INFECTION CAN SPREAD FROM THE UPPER RESPIRATORY TRACT TO THE EAR. 
INFECTION OF THE AUDITORY TUBE CAUSES SWELLING OF THE MUCOUS LININGS, AND THE 
TUBE BECOMES BLOCKED. THIS RESULTS IN DIMINISHED HEARING.

causing infections. You also have to manually remove all 
the secretion from the nose of a small child because 
they cannot properly do that.
9

Vascularization from inside comes from the carotid 
arteries (internal and external). These are a lot of 
branches, and I don't expect you to know the names, 
but I'd like you to know that they form anastomoses. 
These anastomoses come into an area called the 
common area (Kiesselbach area), Common bleeding can 
happen in this area. If people have a problem with the 
nose, the doctor will tell you to raise up your head and 
put pressure in this area between the anastomoses and 
we expect the bleeding to stop. Again, the veins follow 
the arteries so we don't need to talk about that. 
10
VASCULATURE
INTERNAL CAROTID BRANCHES:

ANTERIOR ETHMOIDAL ARTERY

POSTERIOR ETHMOIDAL ARTERY
THE ETHMOIDAL ARTERIES ARE BRANCH OF 
THE OPHTHALMIC ARTERY. 
EXTERNAL CAROTID BRANCHES:

SPHENOPALATINE ARTERY

GREATER PALATINE ARTERY

SUPERIOR LABIAL ARTERY

LATERAL NASAL ARTERIES

THESE ARTERIES FORM ANASTOMOSES WITH EACH OTHER. THIS 
IS PARTICULARLY PREVALENT IN THE ANTERIOR PORTION OF THE 
NOSE 

THE VEINS OF THE NOSE TEND TO FOLLOW THE ARTERIES. THEY 
DRAIN INTO THE PTERYGOID PLEXUS, FACIAL VEIN OR 
CAVERNOUS SINUS.

The common manifestation in clinical that we see is nose 
bleed and we call this epistaxis due to the rich blood 
supply.  This can be local or systemic. Sometimes people 
can hit their head or nose (local), or sometimes they can 
have hypertension (systemic) or just blow their nose very 
harshly. The bleeding is very common in small kids 
because their vasculature is very vulnerable to pressure. 
That's why the doctor would ask you to put pressure on 
the nose or cold compression in order to minimize the 
bleeding.
11
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: EPISTAXIS
 EPISTAXIS IS A NOSEBLEED. DUE TO THE RICH BLOOD SUPPLY OF THE NOSE, THIS IS A 
COMMON OCCURRENCE. IT IS MOST LIKELY TO OCCUR IN THE ANTERIOR THIRD OF THE NASAL 
CAVITY ² THIS AREA IS KNOWN AS THE KIESSELBACH AREA.
 THE CAUSE CAN BE LOCAL (SUCH AS TRAUMA), OR SYSTEMIC (SUCH AS HYPERTENSION).

Innervation from inside can be special or general. Special 
sensation in the nose is the smelling sensation coming 
from the olfactory nerve in the top part of the roof of 
the nose. General sensation is the pain/pressure, 
coming from nasopalatine nerves. And again, anything in 
the nose, we have maxillary V1 and V2, but these are 
different branches than the one outside. So we have the 
nasopalatine nerve (green) coming from the maxillary 
nerve and the nasocellular nerve (blue) coming from the 
ophthalmic nerve. The external nose is also supplied by 
trigeminal nerve (V1 and V2).
12
INNERVATION
 CAN BE FUNCTIONALLY DIVIDED 
INTO SPECIAL AND GENERAL INNERVATION.
 SPECIAL SENSORY SMELL. BY OLFACTORY NERVES. 
 GENERAL SENSORY INNERVATION TO THE SEPTUM 
AND LATERAL WALLS IS DELIVERED BY 
THE NASOPALATINE NERVE (BRANCH OF 
MAXILLARY NERVE) & THE NASOCILIARY 
NERVE (BRANCH OF THE OPHTHALMIC NERVE).
 INNERVATION TO THE EXTERNAL SKIN OF THE NOSE 
IS SUPPLIED BY THE TRIGEMINAL NERVE.

So the larynx, we're not going to talk about it in much 
detail because you will visit this again next year. The 
larynx has three main functions:
1) It acts for air passage.
2) It acts as a sphincter to regulate air and food flow. 
3) It is an organ of phonations for production of sounds. 
13
THE LARYNX
CARTILAGINOUS STRUCTURE IN THE NECK THAT GUARDS THE ENTRANCE TO THE TRACHEA
HAS 3 BASIC FUNCTIONS; IN ORDER OF IMPORTANCE:
1. AIR PASSAGE: CARTILAGINOUS STRUCTURE ENSURES PATENCY OF AIRWAY

Transcription:
-
This block has two histology lectures on the respiratory system. Today covers most of the 
conducting portion, from the nose to the trachea. The remaining parts of the respiratory 
system are covered in the next lecture.
1

The lecture covers the respiratory tract from the nose to the trachea: the conducting and 
respiratory portions, the nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses and pharynx, the difference between 
respiratory and olfactory mucosa, and the structure and function of the larynx and trachea.
Transcription:
-
For today, we have to cover everything from the nose until the trachea. You have to know 
the function and the structure of every organ in this part of the respiratory system.
2

The respiratory system does much more than gas exchange. It conducts and filters air, 
exchanges gases in the alveoli, produces speech in the larynx, gives the sense of smell through 
the olfactory mucosa, has endocrine functions, and regulates immune responses to inhaled 
antigens.
Transcription:
-
The nose is a passage for air to enter, but we also smell using the olfactory portion of the 
nose.
-
The pharynx and larynx keep the airway open. The larynx also makes sound, so speech is 
one of the functions of the respiratory system.
-
In the lung, the first function that comes to mind is gas exchange.
-
There are also immune cells in the respiratory system (lymphocytes, macrophages, mast 
cells) that protect it.
-
Some cells have an endocrine function and release hormones, which we will cover today.
-
So do not only think of air conduction and gas exchange; remember the other functions 
done by different parts of the respiratory system.
3

Structurally, the tract is divided into upper and lower parts according to their embryological 
origin. The upper tract (nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, pharynx) develops from the primitive 
oral cavity. The lower tract (larynx, trachea, bronchi and their divisions, lung) develops from 
the foregut endoderm and its surrounding mesenchyme.
Transcription:
-
Different books include different parts in the upper and lower tract. Here we divide them 
according to where they arise from during embryonic life.
-
The nose, the sinuses and the pharynx are the upper respiratory tract. They all develop from 
the primitive oral cavity.
-
From the larynx until the end of the lung, they arise from the foregut endoderm and the 
surrounding mesenchyme.
o
The endoderm gives rise to the epithelium.
o
The mesenchyme gives rise to the muscle and the cartilage.
-
This will not be our focus at all.
4

Functionally, the tract has a conducting portion (nasal cavities, pharynx, larynx, trachea, 
bronchi, bronchioles and terminal bronchioles) that cleans and humidifies the inspired air and 
provides conduits for air movement, and a respiratory portion (respiratory bronchioles, 
alveolar ducts and alveoli) where gas exchange takes place.
Transcription:
-
Air goes from the nose to the nasopharynx, oropharynx and laryngopharynx, then the 
larynx, then the trachea, which has cartilage in its wall.
-
The trachea divides into the bronchi, which enter the lung and divide many times to give the 
bronchioles.
-
Once alveoli start to protrude from the wall of the bronchiole, gas exchange (respiration) 
can happen from that point.
o
The last bronchiole without alveoli in its wall is the terminal bronchiole.
o
The first bronchiole with alveoli in its wall is the respiratory bronchiole.
-
This is very important, even in the lab: you have to differentiate these two types.
-
Conducting portion: nose, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, and it ends at the terminal 
bronchiole.
-
Respiratory portion: starts with the respiratory bronchiole, then the alveolar ducts and 
alveoli, which are covered next week.
-
You should know which components belong to each portion.
-
The conducting portion cleans the air, humidifies it if it is dry, and controls its temperature if 
it is hot or cold, before it reaches the respiratory portion. The respiratory portion takes in 
oxygen and gets rid of carbon dioxide.
5

The two nasal cavities are separated by a bony and cartilaginous nasal septum. Each is divided 
into three regions: the vestibule, lined by stratified squamous epithelium (skin); the respiratory 
region, lined by respiratory mucosa; and the olfactory region, lined by specialized olfactory 
mucosa.
Transcription:
-
If you touch your nose, the front part is soft because it is made of hyaline cartilage, and the 
back part is supported by bone.
-
Histologically, the nasal cavity is divided into three parts:
o
The vestibule, the part you can touch.
o
The respiratory region, the biggest part of the nasal cavity.
o
The olfactory region, the very apical part.
-
You need to know the lining epithelium of each part.
-
The vestibule is in contact with the external environment, so its lining has to be very 
protective. It is covered by skin (keratinized stratified squamous epithelium). As it goes 
inside, it becomes thinner, loses its keratin and soon changes to respiratory epithelium.
-
Epithelium vs mucosa: when we say the respiratory region is covered by respiratory 
mucosa, the mucosa is made of two structures:
o
The epithelium (pseudostratified columnar epithelium with cilia).
o
The lamina propria. Do not forget it; it is really important.
-
Do not say only epithelium or only lamina propria. The epithelium plus the lamina propria 
together make the mucosa.
6

The vestibule is the dilated space just inside the nostrils. It is lined by skin (stratified squamous 
epithelium) with coarse moist hairs called vibrissae, and sweat and sebaceous glands. 
Posteriorly, the epithelium becomes thinner and changes to pseudostratified columnar 
epithelium.
Transcription:
-
The vestibule is the very early part of the nose immediately inside the nostril. It is covered 
by skin, which we know because it is stratified squamous epithelium.
-
The hairs here are called vibrissae, and we can even see them.
-
As the vestibule becomes the respiratory region, the epithelium first becomes non-
keratinized, then thinner, and then the stratified squamous epithelium becomes 
pseudostratified columnar epithelium.
7

The respiratory region is the largest part (inferior 2/3) of the nasal cavity and is lined by 
respiratory mucosa. The medial wall (nasal septum) is smooth, while the lateral wall has three 
bony projections, the superior, middle and inferior conchae (turbinates). The conchae increase 
the surface area and cause turbulence in the airflow so that the air is conditioned more 
efficiently.
Transcription:
-
The septum is made of hyaline cartilage in its lower front part and bone in its back part.
-
The lateral wall has three bones called the conchae or turbinate bones: inferior, middle and 
superior.
-
We need them to increase the surface area, so the air has time to circulate inside the nose 
to be cleaned, humidified and have its temperature regulated before it reaches the next 
step. Air conditioning happens in this area.
-
The respiratory region is lined by respiratory epithelium with lamina propria under it, so it is 
covered by respiratory mucosa.
8

Respiratory epithelium is pseudostratified columnar ciliated epithelium. Its most abundant cell 
is the ciliated cell (up to 70%): a tall columnar cell whose motile cilia project into the mucus 
covering the surface. Together, the cilia and mucus form the mucociliary escalator, which traps 
particles and sweeps them towards the throat to be swallowed or expelled.
Transcription:
-
There are five cells you have to know in the respiratory epithelium.
-
1. Ciliated cells:
o
Columnar cells with highly motile cilia protruding from the surface.
o
They are the most numerous cells in this epithelium. The nucleus is usually basal and 
oval.
o
The cilia protrude into the mucus covering them. The mucus traps particles like dust, 
and the cilia move to push it out.
o
In the nose, it is not pushed out through the nostril. It is pushed to the pharynx, 
where it is either swallowed or sneezed out.
o
This is called the mucociliary escalator.
9

Goblet cells (5 to 15%) extend through the whole thickness of the epithelium, have basal nuclei 
and an apical part filled with mucinogen granules, lack cilia, and secrete mucus. Brush cells are 
columnar cells with short, blunt microvilli; afferent sensory nerve endings are related to their 
bases, so they act as chemosensory receptors.
Transcription:
-
2. Goblet cells:
o
Flask-shaped with basal flattened nuclei. The upper part is filled with mucin 
granules.
o
When the slide is prepared, these granules dissolve, so we see empty spaces rather 
than the pink content of the cell.
o
Function: synthesizing and secreting mucus.
-
3. Brush cells:
o
The word brush tells you they have microvilli on the surface. They are tall cells.
o
A sensory nerve is related to the base of the cell, which is why they are 
chemosensory receptors. They sense the chemical structure of the air entering the 
nose.
o
They have no cilia.
10

Basal (stem) cells do not reach the surface and divide to give rise to the other epithelial cells. 
Small granule (Kulchitsky) cells resemble basal cells but contain secretory granules and do not 
reach the surface. They are the respiratory representatives of the diffuse neuroendocrine cells 
and release signaling molecules such as serotonin and calcitonin that act on nearby epithelial 
cells, sensory nerves and airway smooth muscle.
Transcription:
-
There are two short cells that never touch the surface.
-
4. Basal (stem) cells:
o
They are the mother cells of all the cells of the respiratory epithelium: columnar, 
brush, goblet and granule cells.
o
They are easy to see with H&E.
-
5. Small granule cells:
o
Their cytoplasm is filled with granules. They look exactly like basal cells and cannot 
reach the surface.
o
They are diffuse neuroendocrine cells. Diffuse means they are scattered between 
the cells rather than forming a gland. Neuroendocrine means they have both nerve-
like and endocrine-like properties.
o
Nerve-like: they respond to the local environment. Endocrine-like: they then release 
signaling molecules such as serotonin that influence the epithelium, smooth muscle 
and sensory nerves around them.
-
So the five cells are: ciliated columnar cells, goblet cells, brush cells, basal (stem) cells and 
small granule cells.
-
You have to know these by heart. Whenever an area is lined by pseudostratified ciliated 
columnar epithelium with goblet cells, it has these five types of cells.
11

The lamina propria of the respiratory region is firmly attached to the periosteum and 
perichondrium of the adjacent bone and cartilage. It is loose connective tissue with a complex 
vasculature of capillary loops and venous plexuses, giving a rich blood flow that warms and 
humidifies the air. It contains mucous glands, many with serous demilunes, that supplement 
the goblet cells.
Transcription:
-
The lamina propria is loose areolar connective tissue with many blood vessels.
-
It is not just small capillaries. There is a complex vascular network of capillary loops and 
venous plexuses under the epithelium. We need this rich blood supply to warm and 
humidify the air entering the nose.
-
You cannot move the mucosa inside your nose because it is firmly attached to the 
perichondrium over the cartilage in front and to the periosteum over the bone at the back.
-
Mucus from goblet cells is not enough, so there are also glands.
o
Reminder from foundation: serous acini make watery secretion, mucous acini make 
thick mucus, and mixed acini make both.
o
The respiratory tract mostly has mixed (seromucous) glands: mucous acini with 
serous demilunes.
o
Their function is to supplement the goblet cells by adding more mucus.
13

The respiratory mucosa of the nasal cavity conditions (climatizes) the air by warming it through 
the vascular network and moistening it. It filters particles through mucous and serous 
secretions together with the vibrissae of the vestibule. It also provides a local immune 
response through lymphocytes, macrophages and mast cells.
Transcription:
-
Conditioning means three things: warming the air, moistening it, and removing particles we 
do not want. This is also called climatization.
-
There are also immune cells (lymphocytes, macrophages and mast cells) in the lamina 
propria of the respiratory region.
-
From the questions:
o
Respiratory epithelium is not simple. It is pseudostratified ciliated columnar 
epithelium with goblet cells.
o
The capillary loops hold a lot of warm blood, which brings cold air towards body 
temperature and adds humidity if the air is dry.
o
The cilia move mucus towards the pharynx, whether they are in the nose or in the 
trachea.
o
Only use keratinized or non-keratinized for stratified squamous epithelium. Do not 
say non-keratinized pseudostratified.
14

Slide 14: Video, mucociliary clearance
Transcription:
-
A short video on mucociliary clearance was shown.
-
The air we breathe contains foreign matter such as dust, bacteria and pollen.
-
Goblet cells secrete viscous mucus that forms a layer to trap foreign material.
-
The wave-like action of the cilia moves the mucus layer, removing the foreign matter and 
preventing it from entering the lungs.
15

The olfactory region is located at the apex (upper 1/3) of the nasal cavity and is lined by 
specialized olfactory mucosa: olfactory epithelium without goblet cells plus lamina propria. Its 
main function is to detect odour.
Transcription:
-
In the upper third of the nasal cavity, the cells look like pseudostratified epithelium, but 
they are totally different from respiratory epithelium. That is why we call it olfactory 
epithelium and the mucosa olfactory mucosa.
-
Its function is detecting odour.
-
Like any epithelium, it has loose areolar connective tissue under it, the lamina propria.
16

The olfactory epithelium is pseudostratified columnar and contains olfactory receptor cells, 
bipolar neurons that span the epithelium and enter the CNS, with immotile cilia carrying the 
odour receptors. Sustentacular (supporting) cells are the most numerous; they have apical 
nuclei and microvilli and give mechanical and metabolic support, synthesizing and secreting 
odorant-binding proteins. Basal cells are stem cells for both receptor and supporting cells. 
Brush cells are also present.
Transcription:
-
1. Olfactory receptor cells (the yellow cells in the figure):
o
They are nerve cells and they are bipolar.
o
They have cilia on the surface, but these cilia are not motile, because their job is 
different: the receptors that bind odours are on these cilia.
-
2. Sustentacular (supporting) cells (the pink cells):
o
Nerve cells cannot work alone, so they need supporting cells. These are like glial 
cells, but we do not call them glia.
o
They support the cells physically and metabolically, by making odorant-binding 
protein, which odours have to attach to. This is very important for the function of 
the sensory cells.
o
They have no cilia, only very short microvilli.
-
3. Basal cells:
o
They are the mother cells of the supporting cells and of the olfactory receptor 
(nerve) cells.
o
This is one of the very rare sites in the body where nerve cells regenerate.
-
4. Brush cells, exactly as in the respiratory epithelium.
17

The olfactory lamina propria lies directly over the periosteum of the underlying bone. It 
contains blood and lymphatic vessels, unmyelinated olfactory nerves, myelinated nerves and 
the olfactory (Bowman) glands. These glands secrete a serous watery fluid that dissolves 
odorous substances so the cilia can detect them, and flushes the surface for new odour stimuli.
Transcription:
-
Are there goblet cells here? No. Thick mucus from goblet cells would block the receptors on 
the cilia.
-
So any gland here cannot produce mucus. It has to be purely serous. These are the 
Bowman glands (olfactory glands).
-
The lamina propria contains the unmyelinated nerves coming from the bipolar receptor 
cells, which penetrate the ethmoid bone to reach the brain.
-
Why the watery secretion matters: it dissolves the odours already attached to the receptors 
and flushes them away, so new odours can attach. This is why, when buying perfume, 
people smell coffee in between.
-
Rule for the lining epithelium, useful for the rest of this lecture and the next:
o
A space that only sees air: respiratory epithelium (pseudostratified ciliated 
columnar).
o
A space that sees air plus food: stratified squamous epithelium.
o
A space with air that does a special, strong job (like producing sound): stratified 
squamous epithelium, to resist friction.
-
By now, you have to know the three parts of the nasal cavity, the lining mucosa of each, the 
differences between them and the cells making them.
19

The four paired paranasal sinuses (frontal, ethmoidal, sphenoidal and maxillary) are air-filled 
spaces in the skull bones that communicate with the nasal cavity through narrow openings. 
They are lined by respiratory epithelium with a thin lamina propria containing a few small 
mucous glands. They decrease the weight of the skull and add resonance to the voice.
Transcription:
-
These spaces only see air, nothing else, so the lining epithelium is respiratory, with lamina 
propria under it.
-
Function: decreasing the skull weight, and the resonance of our voice is made by these 
cavities.
-
I do not care about the names. The most important thing here is the lining epithelium.
20

The pharynx connects the nasal and oral cavities to the larynx and esophagus and is a 
passageway for air and food. The nasopharynx, behind the nasal cavity and connected to the 
middle ears by the Eustachian tubes, is lined by respiratory epithelium, with serous and 
mucous glands and the pharyngeal tonsil in its lamina propria. The oropharynx (behind the oral 
cavity) and laryngopharynx (behind the larynx) are lined by stratified squamous epithelium.
Transcription:
-
The nasopharynx only sees air, so it is lined by respiratory epithelium. If food or water 
reaches it, we feel a burning sensation because this epithelium cannot tolerate it.
-
The oropharynx and laryngopharynx carry food as well as air, so they are lined by stratified 
squamous epithelium.
-
We cannot have keratin inside our body, so it is non-keratinized.
-
You have to know the epithelial lining of each part.
21

The larynx is the air passage between the pharynx and the trachea. It is an irregular 
musculocartilaginous tube lined with mucous membrane (epithelium and lamina propria). It 
produces sound (organ of voice), maintains an open airway, and prevents foreign objects from 
entering the lower respiratory passages.
Transcription:
-
It is irregular and has cartilage and muscles, so we describe it as an irregular 
musculocartilaginous tube.
-
It mostly carries only air, so it is mainly lined by respiratory epithelium.
-
Functions: organ of voice, and keeping the airway open.
-
The epiglottis opens and closes all day to stop food entering the airway.
22

The laryngeal skeleton is formed of irregular plates of hyaline and elastic cartilage connected 
by joints, ligaments and membranes and moved by the intrinsic laryngeal muscles. Hyaline: 
thyroid, cricoid and part of the arytenoid. Elastic: epiglottis, vocal process of the arytenoid, 
cuneiform and corniculate.
Transcription:
-
The most important thing here is which type of cartilage each one is.
-
The big ones, the thyroid and the cricoid, are hyaline, and part of the arytenoid is also 
hyaline.
-
All the rest are elastic.
-
I will really focus on the epiglottis.
23

Slide 22: Video, function of the larynx
Transcription:
-
A video showed how food passes: when food passes, the epiglottis closes so the food does 
not enter the larynx.
24

The epiglottis is a flattened structure projecting from the upper rim of the larynx, with a lingual 
and a laryngeal surface. The lingual surface is covered by stratified squamous epithelium. The 
laryngeal surface is covered by stratified squamous epithelium that changes to pseudostratified 
ciliated columnar epithelium. Mixed mucoserous glands lie beneath the epithelium.
Transcription:
-
The upper surface is close to the tongue, so it is called the lingual surface. The surface 
facing the larynx is the laryngeal surface.
-
The lingual surface faces the food, so it is lined by stratified squamous epithelium.
-
The laryngeal surface has two parts:
o
The anterior part is also stratified squamous, because it is in friction all the time as 
the epiglottis opens and closes.
o
The inner part only sees air, so it is lined by respiratory epithelium.
25

The histology slide shows stratified squamous epithelium on the lingual surface and free 
margin, a transition zone on the laryngeal surface where it changes to respiratory epithelium, 
seromucous acini, and a core of elastic cartilage.
Transcription:
-
Both the lingual surface and the anterior part of the laryngeal surface are lined by stratified 
squamous epithelium, which protects them.
-
Lower down on the laryngeal surface, the lining becomes respiratory (pseudostratified with 
cilia on the surface).
-
The epiglottis opens and closes all the time, so it is very elastic. That is why it has elastic 
cartilage in its core.
-
In the transition, you see many layers with flat surface cells, then all of a sudden cilia start 
to appear.
-
From now on, any gland we see will be mixed: mucous acini with serous demilunes.
26

The laryngeal mucosa forms two pairs of folds separated by an invagination called the 
ventricle. The upper pair, the false vocal cords (vestibular folds), are immobile and covered 
with respiratory epithelium over numerous seromucous glands. The lower pair, the true vocal 
cords (vocal folds), are mobile and important for producing sound.
Transcription:
-
The false vocal cords are mostly not used to make sound. The true vocal cords are the ones 
we use to make sound.
-
The false cord only sees air and does nothing strong, so it is lined by respiratory epithelium.
-
The true vocal cord is covered by stratified squamous epithelium. This is very important. 
We need a stronger epithelium that resists friction.
27

The true vocal cord consists of (1) nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium, which 
resists mechanical stress and friction from vibration; (2) the superficial layer of the lamina 
propria; (3) the vocal ligament, a dense regular bundle of elastic connective tissue; and (4) the 
vocalis muscle, a bundle of striated muscle that regulates the tension of the fold and its 
ligament and helps produce sounds of different frequencies.
Transcription:
-
Layers from outside in:
o
Stratified squamous epithelium. This is the only part in this area lined by stratified 
squamous epithelium.
o
Lamina propria, as usual.
o
The vocal ligament: dense regular bundle of elastic connective tissue.
o
The vocalis muscle: we can control it when we talk, so it is skeletal muscle.
-
Some people can make their voice much higher or lower pitched by controlling this muscle.
28

The histology slide shows the false vocal cord lined by respiratory epithelium over seromucous 
glands, and the true vocal cord lined by stratified squamous epithelium with the skeletal vocalis 
muscle beneath.
Transcription:
-
False vocal cord: respiratory epithelium, with very clear acini underneath.
-
True vocal cord: stratified squamous epithelium, and inside it the muscle with multiple 
peripheral nuclei, which is skeletal muscle: the vocalis.
-
From the questions:
o
What you see at the back of the mouth is the uvula, not the epiglottis.
o
The trachea keeps the airway open, but the larynx does this too.
o
Secretions moved by the cilia, from the nose or the trachea, go to the pharynx. 
There they are either swallowed (and the HCl in the stomach kills whatever reaches 
it) or sneezed out.
29

The trachea is a short, flexible tube about 10 to 12 cm long that extends from the larynx and 
ends at the carina by dividing into the two main (primary) bronchi. It conducts air, its wall helps 
condition the inspired air, and its lumen stays open because of its series of cartilage rings.
Transcription:
-
The trachea runs from the larynx and bifurcates at the carina to give the bronchi.
-
Behind the trachea is the esophagus.
-
The C-shaped hyaline cartilage leaves the posterior part without cartilage. This is important 
for function: if cartilage were there, we could not swallow a big bolus of food. The soft 
posterior wall adapts to it.
-
Function: a conduit for air that keeps the airway open.
30

The tracheal wall has four layers. The first is the mucosa: respiratory epithelium on a thick 
basement membrane of densely packed collagen fibres, and a lamina propria of loose 
connective tissue rich in elastic and collagen fibres. The lamina propria is very cellular 
(lymphocytes, plasma cells, fibroblasts) and has diffuse and nodular lymphatic tissue equivalent 
to BALT.
Transcription:
-
There are four layers, and you have to be very careful with each one.
-
The trachea only carries air, so the lining is respiratory epithelium. We cannot say anything 
else.
-
Unique here: a very thick basement membrane made of dense collagen, clearly visible 
under the epithelium.
-
The lamina propria is loose areolar connective tissue with blood vessels and many 
lymphocytes.
-
Sometimes lymphocytes form BALT (bronchus-associated lymphatic tissue): lymphatic 
nodules like those in the lymph node and spleen, found in the lamina propria and 
submucosa of the trachea, bronchi and bronchioles.
31

The submucosa is loose connective tissue slightly denser than the lamina propria; the boundary 
between them is the elastic membrane. It contains diffuse lymphatic tissue and nodules, the 
larger vessels and lymphatics of the tracheal wall, and mucus-secreting acini with serous 
demilunes, which are numerous in the cartilage-free posterior gap.
Transcription:
-
The submucosa is connective tissue with blood vessels, a lot of collagen and elastic fibres, 
and glands.
-
Except for the olfactory region, which has the only purely serous glands, every part has 
mucous glands with serous demilunes.
-
The elastic membrane is a very dense layer of elastic fibres. Once you see it, the lamina 
propria has ended and the submucosa has started.
-
Not every slide in the lab shows the elastic membrane, but you should know it.
32

The cartilaginous layer has 16 to 20 C-shaped hyaline rings that give flexibility and keep the 
lumen open. Their open ends face posteriorly against the esophagus and are bridged by smooth 
muscle (the trachealis muscle) and a sheet of fibroelastic tissue attached to the perichondrium; 
some seromucous acini are also present. The adventitia is loose connective tissue binding the 
trachea to adjacent structures.
Transcription:
-
The cartilage is C-shaped hyaline cartilage (16 to 20 rings, as on the slide).
-
The posterior part has no cartilage. Instead, it has muscle we cannot control, so it is smooth 
muscle, called the trachealis, with some fibroelastic tissue.
-
The last layer is the adventitia.
-
When I say respiratory epithelium in the trachea, you have to know the five cells 
mentioned at the beginning, because they are here too.
33

Inflammation of any of these organs is named by adding "-itis": rhinitis, sinusitis, pharyngitis, 
adenoiditis, laryngitis. In rhinitis, the vascular network of the lamina propria becomes engorged 
and leaky, causing marked swelling of the mucosa that narrows the air passage. SARS-CoV-2 
anosmia is transient: the virus binds to and depletes the supporting cells, and smell is usually 
restored within 10 days.
Transcription:
-
In rhinitis, the nose is very congested because the vascular network in the lamina propria 
becomes engorged. This is the feeling we get with flu.
-
During COVID, many people lost their smell (anosmia).
o
At first it was thought the problem was in the nerve cells, but it was in the 
supporting cells, because they make the odorant-binding protein.
o
Smell returned to normal after some days (the lecturer said 10 to 30 days; the slide 
says within 10 days in most cases).
34

A singer's nodule is a benign reactive polyp of the stratified squamous epithelium of the true 
vocal cords that affects the voice.
Transcription:
-
You do not need to study the pathology of these diseases, but you should know what they 
are and which organ is affected, because they appear in case scenarios.
-
Singer's nodules occur on the vocal cord, usually on its free margin, in people who talk a lot: 
singers, teachers, professors.
-
They are benign protrusions of the epithelium. The true vocal cord is lined by stratified 
squamous epithelium, which is why the nodule is made of stratified squamous epithelium.
35

Think of the tank as a pump like the heart. Let’s say the fluid in it is blood and that 
the measuring cylinders are organs. 
(Usually the heart beats at 5L/min, but for the sake of explanation it’s 1L/min)
There is a differential pressure in the arteries (delta P) because without a 
differential pressure there will be no blood flow.
A: The blood flow is equal for every organ.
B: ONE of the arterioles gets dilated so there is increased blood flow to one of 
the organs (let’s say skeletal muscle for the sake of explanation). The pressure in 
the capillaries in the skeletal muscle will INCREASE which will lead to a 
DECREASE in the Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP) which is the delta P. 
C: With time, a regulatory factors comes to regulate delta P so that the blood 
keeps going to the skeletal muscle but the value of delta P changes. This needs 
to happen because this is now a completely open arteriole, so not all the blood

to this tissue. As a reflex, the arteriolar systems in other organs will constrict to 
reduce blood flow to their systems. This is to maintain blood flow to the brain. 
The blood flow to the brain remains unchanged to maintain adequate blood

Cardiac Output is ALWAYS 5L in both systemic and pulmonary circulation. 
The Systolic BP is 5-6 times less in the pulmonary circulation because of the 
different circulations next to the heart. 
7

Nervous Regulation of the Circulation
8

CARDIAC INDEX AT DIFFERENT AGES
Cardiac Index= Cardiac Output/Body surface area
Cardiac output = Venous return
Factors that directly affect CO:
1. Metabolism
2. Exercising
3. Age 
4. Body size
The doctor said this is something VERY important.
The Cardiac Index is the Cardiac Output per body surface area. 
Cardiac Output could differ between someone obese and someone thin. A thin 
person has less surface area to cover and less tissues to nourish, so is less 
Cardiac Output. 
Cardiac Output increases sharply during development and decline slowly with 
age. This is because metabolism changes with age. Exercise and body size 
change too. 
The Four Factors that Affect Cardiac Output:
1. Metabolism 
2. Exercise 
3. Age 
4. Body Size 
9

The doctor emphasized the formula 
CARDIAC OUTPUT = VENOUS RETURN 
Whatever leaves the heart has to come back to the heart because it is a closed 
circulation, unless there is hemorrhage (blood loss). 
Increased Cardiac Output = Increased Venous Return , and vice versa
9

DOES THE HEART OR
PERIPHERAL
CIRCULATION CONTROL
CARDIAC OUTPUT?
The Frank-Starling Law Of The Heart
Factors that increase cardiac pumping:
1. Increased venous return
2. Stretch of the SA node
3. Stretch of the atria (Bainbridge reflex)
Cardiac output = venous return
The Venous Return is the blood coming into the right atrium and the Cardiac 
Output is the blood leaving through the Aorta. 
Increasing Venous Return will cause a stretch in the thin muscle of the atrial wall 
which will exert a pressure on the wall. This stretch will elicit a reflex called the 
Bainbridge Reflex. This stretch will stimulate the increase in the activity of the 
sympathetic nervous system. 
This overload of blood into the right atrium will stretch the SA node which can 
also lead a reflex that will increase sympathetic activity. Therefore, there will be 
an immediate increase in the Cardiac Output. There will be more blood coming 
into the right atrium which is immediately compensated for the by the blood 
increased amount of blood leaving the left ventricle. 
Since there is no communication between the right and left ventricle, all of this is 
done by the sympathetic activity that acts as a link between the two ventricles to 
regulate Venous Return and Cardiac Output. 
Apparently, this is one way of looking at the Frank-Starling Law. 
10

CO IS THE SUM OF ALL TISSUE BLOOD FLOWS
• Cardiac
Output
is
the
sum
of
all
tissue flows and is affected by their regulation
(CO = 5L/min, cardiac index = 3L/min/m2).
• CO is proportional to tissue O2 use
• CO is proportional to 1/TPR when AP is constant
•
CO = (MAP - RAP) / TPR
Cardiac Output is the sum of all the outputs from the different tissues in the 
body.
Everything that leaves the heart from the left side will come back from the right 
side which means that the Cardiac Output at the aortic level is equal to the 
Venous Return at the venous level.
Cardiac Output is 5L/min (memorize this)
Cardiac Index is 3L/min/m^2
Cardiac Output is: 
1. proportional to the use of oxygen in the tissues 
The biggest tissue is skeletal muscle, so if someone is exercising more than 
normal, there is an increase in Cardiac Output to accommodate for the tissue’s 
needs 
2.   inversely proportional to the Total Peripheral Resistance when the Atrial 
Pressure is constant.  
The Total Peripheral Resistance is dictated for by the constriction of the 
11

arterioles right before the capillaries. Increase in TPR will increase Cardiac 
Output and vice versa 
Under normal conditions at rest, MAP = CO x TPR. We don’t usually consider the 
Right Atrial Pressure because RAP is close to zero. However, if we increase the 
venous return then the right atrial pressure will increase and can no longer be 
ignored. Therefore, the Cardiac Output is equal to the MAP at the left side of the 
heart minus the right atrial pressure over the Total Peripheral Resistance. TPR is 
the resistance generated by all the arterioles in all the tissues of the body.                   
11

• CO is proportional to 1/TPR when AP is constant
•
AP = CO X TPR
The arteries recoil during systole and diastole (Mean Arterial Pressure). 
Arterioles work as resistance controllers. The more they are constricted, the 
higher the resistance, the higher the mean arterial pressure, the higher the 
cardiac output. This is called the Total Peripheral Resistance. 
Look at the graph
A person with anemia has less red blood cells so less oxygen is delivered to the 
tissues. The TPR is so low because more blood needs to be brought to the 
tissues so the Cardiac Output is higher than normal.    
The doctor said he won’t ask questions about the graph. It’s just for 
understanding. 
12

THE HEART HAS LIMITS FOR THE CO THAT IT CAN ACHIEVE
•
Sympathetic 
- Increasing heart rate
- Increasing strength of contraction
•
Heart hypertrophy
- increased strength of contraction (almost 
double)
Sympathetic + hypertrophy          CO = 40 L/min which will 
determine the running time of a marathon runner. 
Causes of Hypereffective heart
This graph shows the activity of the sympathetic nervous system on the Cardiac 
Output curve. 
Atrial pressure is on the x-axis because Atrial Pressure is an indication of Venous 
Return. Normal Right Atrial Pressure is zero. On the graph, if you draw a vertical 
line from 0 on the x-axis, you get a Cardiac Output of 5L/min which is normal.
Memorize the axes on the graph. Very important graph. 
Moving to the right on the graph (increasing Right Atrial Pressure), means more 
Venous Return and more Cardiac Output until it reaches a plateau because the 
heart has a certain capacity. It cannot go beyond a certain limit. (Normal Cardiac 
Output at plateau is about 12L/min) 
However, if a person is hyperactive (an athlete), there is hypereffectivity. In this 
case, a small increase in the Right Atrial Pressure results in a tremendous 
increase in Cardiac Output. 
Conversely, people that live sedentary lives will show hypoeffectivity. This 
13

means that increasing the Venous Return does not show a plateau at the normal 
range. 
In all three conditions, the Cardiac Output at rest is normal.
13

THE HEART HAS LIMITS FOR THE CO THAT IT CAN ACHIEVE
Causes of Hypoeffective heart
He reads the slide
14

PATHOLOGICAL LOW OR HIGH CARDIAC OUTPUT
Refer to the book page 249-250 for the description of the explained conditions of the figure 20-7
We will not be asked about these conditions, it’s just for our information. 
Beri-Beri = high CO
Cardiac shock = low CO
15

THE VENOUS RETURN
The Venous Return is the amount coming into the heart through either the 
superior or inferior vena cava and goes into the right atrium. If Venous Return 
increases, it stretches the right atrium. If it decreases, it does not stretch the 
atrium. 
16

THREE FACTORS REGULATE THE VENOUS RETURN
Mean Systemic Fillling Pressure
VERY IMPORTANT
Venous Return can be regulated by three major factors:
1. Right Atrial Pressure. It’s usually zero, but it can be affected by several 
factors. It can increase if there is an increase in the amount of blood staying 
in the right atrium. The Venous Return is now working against a certain Atrial

tissues. The higher the rate of filling of the right atrium, the higher the Right

through Mean Systemic Filling Pressure. 
3. Resistance to blood flow. This is the resistance between the peripheral 
vessels in the right atrium. Calcification of the veins of formation of plaques 
will induce a resistance to blood flow, impede the Venous Return. It will

against the Venous Return. Therefore, the Venous Return will decrease.

Increasing the blood volume due to an infusion will increase the Mean Systemic 
Filling Pressure. This is because the veins will be distended, so there is lower 
resistance in these blood vessels. The Venous Curve is rotated upwards and to 
the right. 
At point A (under normal conditions at rest), the Cardiac Output and the Venous 
Return cross when the Right Atrial Pressure is 0. This is because Cardiac Output 
is equal to Venous Return. 
If Mean Systemic Filling Pressure is increased to 16 mmHg, the shift in the 
Venous Return curve to the right gives rise to new circulatory dynamics at B. This 
is where both Cardiac Output and Venous Return cross each other. Cardiac 
Output is a little over 12 which is not normal. 
The Atrial Pressure is very high because the Mean Systemic Filling Pressure is 
increased, so there’s more blood going back to the right atrium. If we infuse

increase immediately. 
23

To compensate for this right shift in the Venous Return curve:
1. There is an immediate increase in Capillary Pressure. This means there is 
filtration going on, so the water tends to leave the capillaries and go into the 
interstitial space. 
2. There is Stress-Relaxation induced mainly by the Smooth Muscle Cells to 
compensate for the increased blood volume. 
3. There is also an increased resistance to Venous Returns through the 
peripheral tissue by auto regulation. 
All three of these situations are acute. In about 30 minutes after the infusion, the 
Cardiac Output will return to normal, so the Venous Return curve will return to 
normal. 
Cardiac Output curves and Venous Return curves have upper limits and lower

which Cardiac Output is equal to Venous Return. If there is a fluctuation, there

In the human body, the Arterial Pressure has to be regulated very quickly. It is 
very normal for it to increase and decrease, but it can be problematic if it’s not 
well maintained.
This is why we have internal systems, internal sensors, internal reflexes and 
internal receptors that all work together to restore irregular Arterial Pressure. 
This is mainly done by Baroreceptors & Chemoreceptors, The Atria & The 
Lungs, The Kidneys and The Brain. 
If one of them stops working, it doesn’t necessarily mean that all the others will 
be shut down.

of the body

the heart

Nervous regulation of the circulation
All these systems can be decreased by the nervous system. 
Rapid control of the Arterial Pressure is emphasized a lot by the Baroreceptors.

The Cardiac Output is the blood leaving the heart. Arterial Pressure is equal to 
the Total Peripheral Resistance times the Cardiac Output. 
MAP = CO x TPR
This means that if we increase the TPR, we decrease the MAP. This is done by 
constricting the arterioles which are the sites of regulating resistance for 
circulation. This increases the resistance in large blood vessels like the veins 
which will increase Venous Return and push more blood from the blood 
reservoirs (veins) into the Right Atrium of the heart. 
We can also directly increase Cardiac Output by directly increasing the heart 
rate and the contractility of the ventricles by the sympathetic nerve system.

Sympathetic Nervous System
Vasoconstriction of small arteries and arterioles increases their resistance to
blood flow and decreases blood flow to the tissues.
Vasoconstriction of veins decrease their blood volume and pushes more blood
into the heart (increase venous return).

vasoconstriction
Every time the sympathetic nervous system fires, we can constrict the arteries 
and veins, but more importantly the arterioles. This will increase the resistance 
to blood flow, thereby increasing the Mean Arterial Pressure. 
The same thing happens when you constrict the veins or venules, so more blood 
is going back into the heart.

Parasympathetic Nervous System
The Parasympathetic nervous system plays a minor role in regulating
vascular function in most tissues. Its effect is mainly to reduce the
heart rate and contraction through the Vagus nerve on the figure.
The parasympathetic nervous system goes from the spinal cord to different 
blood vessels and to the heart. 
The sympathetic fibers going to the myocardium (SA node). The 
parasympathetic fibers are mainly firing to the SA node and the AV node. 
We have the Vagus nerve going only to the SA node and the AV node while the
