Effect
Nervous control is by far the most rapid mechanism for arterial pressure regulation.
Sympathetic: increase BP by two times within 5- 10 sec
Parasympathetic: decrease BP by one half within 10 -40 sec.
The more the arterioles are constricted, the greater the resistance. Constriction 
of these arterioles will increase the Mean Arterial Pressure. Constriction of the 
veins and large vessels will increase Venous Return to the heart. 
We can enhance cardiac contractility simply by direct activation of the 
sympathetic fibers that will work on the myocardium to increase the pumping 
activity in the human body. 
When the sympathetic nervous system is active, it can create a 2-fold increase 
in blood pressure in as little 5-10 seconds. When the parasympathetic nervous 
system is active, it can decrease the blood pressure to half in as little as 10-40 
seconds. 
A person is doing exercise or going through emotional stress will have a high 
Mean Arterial Pressure which needs to be regulated quickly. We have all the 
necessary tool to accomplish that.

Relationship between MAP and baroreceptor firing
The higher is the MAP, the higher is the firing rate of the baroreceptor cells.
On this graph, you have the Baroreceptor Action Potential Frequency plotted

Increased Mean Arterial Pressure will increase the firing rate of the arterial 
baroreceptors. This has two consequences. 
1. Decreased sympathetic activity to the heart, arterioles and veins.

Baroreceptors response to Haemorrhage
Very important!
VERY IMPORTANT!!!!
One example of an acute decrease in blood pressure is hemorrhage. Volume of 
blood decreases so the Mean Arterial Pressure decreases. Therefore, there is a 
decrease in firing rate by the baroreceptors resulting in a decreased 
parasympathetic discharge to the heart and increased sympathetic discharge to 
the heart, veins and arterioles. 
The arterioles constrict. Cardiac Output increases, Venous Return increases. 
The heart contracts more. There is an increased Total Peripheral Resistance. 
Mean Arterial Pressure increases. More Mean Arterial Pressure, more 
Baroreceptor firing rate.

Response of the Baroreceptor to Arterial Pressure:
Baroreceptors at the carotid arteries are sensitive to
small changes in pressure but do no operate in ranges
between 0 and 50-60 mmHg (maximum response at 180
mmHg). The aortic baroreceptors are activated at arterial
pressure levels about 30 mmHg higher than the carotid
arteries baroreceptors.
In the normal operating range of arterial pressure, a
slight change in pressure causes a strong change in
baroreflex signals. The rate of firing of baroreflex signals
changes during each systole and diastole.
The high pressure baroreceptors at the carotid arteries are sensitive to small 
changes in pressure. However, they will not operate in low pressure conditions. 
There needs to be a minimum of 70-80 mmHg for the baroreceptors to detect a 
pressure. Their maximum response is 180 mmHg. 
Hypertensive patients can have a blood pressure that exceeds 180 mmHg, so it 
is possible that baroreceptors may not be involved in hypertension regulation. 
The baroreceptors at the aortic arch operate at a pressure about 30 mmHg 
greater than the carotid arteries. This is because the pressure at the aortic arch is 
very high.

After the baroreceptors reflex enter the nucleus tractus solitarius of the
Medullae oblongata, secondary signals inhibit the vasoconstrictor center and
excite the parasympathetic center. Results:

The action potentials from the baroreceptors go to the Nuclear Tractus

Pressure “Buffer” function of the baroreceptor control 
system 
VERY VERY IMPORTANT!
Baroreceptors have plasticity. This means that they have a buffer zone. The 
blood pressure fluctuates between 80 and 120, and the baroreceptors maintain 
the blood pressure in this range.
If the baroreceptors are denervated, the blood pressure can fluctuate in a much 
larger range because the baroreceptors have become defective. 
The baroreceptors maintain the blood pressure at about a third of what it would 
be if they were denervated. E.g. The pulse pressure of the denervated

The fluctuation isn’t on every beat.

the

capacity to consider long-time values as normal values.

Stretch receptors of the atria increase the heart rate by almost 75%. 15%

Increased cerebrospinal fluid in the cranial vault compress the brain and the

point so we call this “the last ditch stand”. It involves such a strong activation

occlusion in a peripheral vessel because all the blood flow needs to be directed 
to the brain. 
If you have a buildup of CSF in the brain, the cranial vault will compress the 
arteries in the vein creating an ischemic response to increase the atrial pressure 
and restore the blood flow. This is the Cushing reaction.

When skeletal muscles contract during exercise, they compress the blood vessels

water you increase the blood volume, and you go back to D. The green curve in D is a partially recovered 
heart, because of the acute sympathetic stimulation and the water retention by the kidneys. 
At D, cardiac output is 5 L/min. This is normal, but the heart is not normal. How do we differentiate A from 
D? By comparing the right atrial pressure. At any moment, if you have a normal cardiac output of 5 L/min 
but a high right atrial pressure, you immediately know that this is a failing heart. It is back to normal 
because of two compensatory mechanisms:  
1. very acute and strong sympathetic stimulation, which is not enough to restore the cardiac output 
completely to 5 L/min, and therefore  
2. the help of the kidneys, which increase the blood volume by retaining more water. 
To summarise: point A is normal (right atrial pressure 0, cardiac output 5). At B (acutely damaged heart) 
cardiac output is less than 2 to 4 and right atrial pressure is very high. With sympathetic compensation we 
move to C, with a higher cardiac output (maybe 4) and higher right atrial pressure. With water retention by 
the kidney we move to D: normal cardiac output, but not a normal right atrial pressure.

Chronic Compensation 
There are two degrees of compensation that happen chronically. This is not acute like the sympathetic 
activity: it takes longer to happen and it stays for a long time. 
1. Fluid retention by the kidneys. 
2. Remodelling of the heart over weeks (various degrees of recovery of the heart). 
Renal fluid retention 
If urine output is lowered with decreased cardiac output, it could shut down completely. We call this 
condition anuria: people will not produce urine anymore. This happens if cardiac output is 50 to 60% less 
than normal. At point B it is less than 50%, but anuria does not necessarily develop at point C. Above these 
values, if cardiac output is still not 5 L/min, the amount of urine formed will be reduced by retaining water. 
When you retain more water in the body, this water will be mainly in the blood vessels. This increases the 
mean systemic filling pressure by increasing two things: (1) the blood volume, and (2) the stretch of the 
veins. By stretching the veins you reduce the venous resistance, which facilitates blood flow to the heart. 
This is point D.

Is fluid retention good or bad for the heart? If it is excessive, it is detrimental. If the failing heart is not 
treated, long-term fluid retention becomes detrimental: 
• 
It greatly increases the workload on an already damaged heart. This is not a normal pump; it is a 
pump with reduced function. 
• 
It overstretches the cardiac muscle. The ventricle can hold only a certain end-diastolic volume, and 
if this increases a lot, the cardiac muscle is overstretched. 
• 
It can cause pulmonary edema, because the pump is not clearing the blood efficiently and the 
pulmonary circulation is filled with blood for longer than it should be. 
• 
It causes extensive edema, not only in the heart but in several parts of the body. Severe edema can 
lead to death. 
The blood stays longer in the veins, venules and capillaries. We saw that if the blood volume in the 
capillaries is increased, the hydrostatic pressure rises, so more water goes into filtration. The lymphatic 
system has a certain plasticity and will absorb more water, but it has a limit beyond which it fails. When it 
fails, water builds up in the interstitial space and we develop edema in all parts of the body. This does not 
develop acutely in acute heart failure; it develops with long-term fluid retention.

Look at a heart damaged by myocardial occlusion. This area is a scar. Immediately, blood vessels will 
develop to irrigate the ischaemic part. We call this angiogenesis, and we call the result a collateral blood

Compensated vs Decompensated Heart Failure 
On the graph, A is not the same A as before; it is simply a chronological order. We start with a normal 
cardiac output curve, then damage to the heart. 
Who kicks in first in acute failure? The sympathetic system. We did not reach 5 L/min. Who kicks in later 
and starts retaining more water? The kidneys. We move to a point which is 5 L/min. However, in the 
second graph, at C, it is not 5 L/min. I have exhausted the sympathetic response, and I have exhausted the 
water retention by the kidneys, and I did not reach 5 L/min. So I ask for more water retention. The more I 
retain water, the more the right atrial pressure increases (moving from B to C to D). The more I increase the 
right atrial pressure, the more detrimental it is for venous return and for cardiac output. 
Because I did not reach 5 L/min, with time this damaged heart is damaged more and more, because I am 
filling it with so much volume that it cannot work. It deteriorates, fails more and more, and the person will 
end up dying. A person with such a circulatory dynamic who never reaches 5 L/min is going into 
decompensated heart failure. 
In decompensated heart failure, cardiac output is not increasing enough. It starts to decrease while right 
atrial pressure increases more and more. We never reach 5 L/min, so the kidney never shuts down its water 
retention. We increase the blood volume more and more, the right atrial pressure more and more, and the 
overload on the heart. The overload keeps increasing until the heart goes into complete failure. 
So there is a huge difference between the two graphs. In the first, we have increased right atrial pressure 
but cardiac output is back to normal: compensated heart failure. In the second, we could not bring cardiac 
output back to normal and the heart fails more and more: decompensated heart failure.

Treatment of Decompensated Heart Failure 
Not everyone with decompensated heart failure will die, because we can treat it. I will not go into the 
details of the drugs, the dosage and when to take them, but I will give one example. 
Digitalis (digoxin), a cardiotonic. Consider the plasma membrane of the cardiomyocyte of the failing heart. 
It has a sodium–potassium pump. Digoxin inhibits the sodium–potassium pump. Less sodium goes outside, 
so sodium increases intracellularly. This increase in intracellular sodium affects the movement of calcium 
through the sodium–calcium exchanger. The exchanger will not bring sodium inside anymore because 
intracellular sodium is already high, and by not bringing in more sodium it will not expel calcium to the 
outside. We then have more calcium in the cardiomyocytes, which increases the force of contraction. 
To repeat: digoxin inhibits the sodium–potassium pump; this leads to more intracellular sodium, which 
affects the movement of calcium through the sodium–calcium exchanger; more calcium inside increases 
the force of contraction. 
Diuretics. Another way to treat decompensated heart failure is to give a diuretic, so the patient urinates 
more and loses more water in the urine. This reduces the blood volume.

Unilateral Heart Failure (Left Ventricle) 
Here the left ventricle alone fails. The right ventricle is fine, but the left ventricle is not pumping blood 
adequately out. The left atrium is linked to the pulmonary circulation, so the pulmonary capillary pressure 
increases. It goes above 28 mmHg, which, if you remember, is the colloid osmotic pressure in the plasma. If 
you do the calculation for the hydrostatic pressures, you will see that fluid will always filter out of the 
capillaries. The lymphatics and the lungs cannot accommodate this huge, constant increase in filtration, so 
the lungs fill with water. 
If this happens acutely and very fast, the build-up of water in the alveoli impairs oxygen exchange between 
the air and the circulation, and the person can suffocate and die within 20 to 30 minutes. Patients with 
water build-up in the lungs who do not die have the chronic form, which builds up slowly with time and 
which needs to be treated with a diuretic.

S L I D E  2 1  
 
Low-Output Cardiac Failure (Cardiogenic Shock) 
If the heart is constantly exposed to slow, progressive deterioration (the causes are many), it becomes 
incapable of pumping the minimal amount of blood required to keep the body alive. 
A normal heart pumps adequately, and venous return and mean systemic filling pressure are normal. In a 
failing heart the pumping is very little and the mean systemic filling pressure immediately increases. This is 
a problem because you need an arterial pressure of 80 mmHg so that the coronary arteries can bring blood 
to the myocardium. If arterial pressure goes below 45 mmHg, you cannot perfuse the coronary arteries 
anymore. This becomes a vicious circle and the heart goes into cardiac shock.

S L I D E  2 2  
 
Other examples of deterioration: 
• 
Increased preload. The mean systemic filling pressure rises, for example when the kidneys retain 
more water. The heart is already failing and now I am increasing the preload, so it fails further and 
further. 
• 
Increased afterload. Everything is fine at the kidneys and the mean systemic filling pressure does 
not rise further, but something happens at the aorta, for example a stenosis or vasoconstriction. 
This is an increase in afterload and the heart deteriorates further and further.

S L I D E  2 3  
 
Treatment of this vicious circle: 
1. Give digitalis immediately. 
2. Infuse whole blood or plasma, or a blood-pressure-raising drug. 
3. Remove the clot from the coronary arteries surgically, or by catheter with a stent placed in the 
coronary artery, then put the person on clot-dissolving (anticoagulant) factors to make sure the clot 
does not return.

Why Acute Heart Failure Does Not Cause Immediate Edema 
The graph shows normal cardiac output (half, then zero) against pressures: mean aortic (arterial) pressure, 
capillary pressure and right atrial pressure. If cardiac output is reduced, mean aortic pressure goes down 
and right atrial pressure goes up. The capillary pressure goes down from about 17 or 18 to 13 mmHg when 
cardiac output is zero. 
We said the veins have a mean systemic filling pressure; we have something similar for the capillaries. If 
nothing is moving at all, with no pumping activity of the heart, the blood in the capillaries will have a 
pressure of about 13 mmHg. This will not cause filtration, because the interstitial space has its own 
hydrostatic pressure and the blood has an oncotic pressure as well. So water will not go outside 
immediately. With time, if this changes, we will have water retention and edema. Acutely, no; chronically, 
yes.

When there is edema in a patient with cardiac failure, there is also a factor released from the atria. Because 
the atria are very stretched, with water retention their muscle starts to secrete atrial natriuretic peptide 
(ANP); other textbooks call it atrial natriuretic factor (ANF), which is exactly the same thing. The increase in 
atrial pressure releases it, and it acts on the kidney to stimulate the secretion of water and salt. This is a 
kind of natural protection: when there is so much stress on the right atrium, it asks the kidneys to reduce 
the load on the heart.

Late-Stage Heart Failure: The Vicious Circle 
Damming of blood in the lungs (as in unilateral left ventricular failure) leads to pulmonary edema. This 
water building up in the alveoli affects the exchange of oxygen with the circulation, so there is less 
oxygenated blood. The cardiac muscle needs oxygen to pump more and is working harder, but it is 
damaged and has less oxygen. This further increases venous return, which is an increase in preload on a 
heart that is already deteriorating and not receiving enough oxygen. All these steps are accentuated, and 
the vicious circle goes on and on. It will not stop by itself until the person dies. 
Immediate treatment by the cardiologist: 
• 
Tourniquets on the arms and legs to sequester blood in the veins. This decreases venous return and 
therefore the workload. 
• 
A rapidly acting diuretic to reduce the blood volume. 
• 
Pure oxygen inhaled by the patient. 
• 
A rapidly acting cardiotonic such as digitalis. 
I do not ask you about these treatments, but when I talk about them you relate them back to the problem 
and understand the problem again and again.

Cardiac Reserve 
I want your full attention on two very important points. The first is that there is a reduction in cardiac 
reserve in compensated heart failure. 
What is cardiac reserve? The graph shows people with different conditions: normal athletes have a very 
high cardiac reserve; moderate coronary disease is less than normal; severe coronary thrombosis is well 
below normal; and other problems show a fluctuating cardiac reserve. Cardiac reserve is the distance from 
point A on the line to the maximum. It is the ability of the heart to respond to the stress of the body. 
Example of stress: exercise. A person with a cardiac output of 5 L/min starts to exercise. As I showed you in 
the previous lecture, it can increase up to 17 L/min, a two-and-a-half-fold increase, until it reaches a 
plateau. This adaptation from point A to the plateau is the cardiac reserve. An athlete could have a cardiac 
output of up to 25 L/min before plateauing. 
Now look at points B, C and D, and mainly D. How much is the distance between D and the plateau? Zero. 
The cardiac output at D is 5 L/min, which is normal, but can this person exercise? Of course not. This is why 
we call it compensated heart failure: a person with 5 L/min and a high right atrial pressure has a 
compensated heart failure, a partially recovered heart, with zero cardiac reserve. These people cannot 
exercise because their heart cannot accommodate them.

The Digitalised Heart 
This is the cardiac output curve of a digitalised heart. The person was on the black curve, going into 
decompensation, and was immediately given digitalis. The cardiac output curve shifts upward. The venous 
return curve after the first day of decompensation is shifted to the right; several days after digitalisation 
there is a shift to the left. This gives a reduction in the mean systemic filling pressure, but it is still not 
normal: usually it is 7, now it is around 11 to 12. This is a new venous return curve and a new cardiac 
output curve. 
The originally decompensated failing heart became a compensated failing heart with the aid of digitalis. But 
look: in this compensated heart failure there is no cardiac reserve (very, very little, which is nothing). A 
person with compensated heart failure has one curve, a person with decompensation has another, and if 
we give digitalis we can revert the decompensation into compensated heart failure. We reach a new 
equilibrium with 5 L/min of cardiac output and venous return, but with an increased mean systemic filling 
pressure and an increased right atrial pressure.
